items.stem: Which historian argued in “The Origins of the Second World War” (1961) that Hitler was an opportunist rather than a planner?
options: Richard Overy
A. J. P. Taylor
Hugh Trevor-Roper
Fritz Fischer
items.answer: A. J. P. Taylor
items.markingKey: B. Taylor’s thesis caused a major controversy.

items.stem: Explain the difference between “to what extent” and “evaluate”.
items.answer: Both require judgement; “evaluate” asks for the strengths and limitations of something to be weighed, while “to what extent” asks how far a claim is valid and requires a clear position on the degree.
items.markingKey: Both require judgement; “evaluate” asks for the strengths and limitations of something to be weighed, while “to what extent” asks how far a claim is valid and requires a clear position on the degree. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "In a compare-and-contrast essay you should write about the first case and then the second." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Effective answers use an integrated structure, comparing the cases point by point throughout the essay.
items.markingKey: Effective answers use an integrated structure, comparing the cases point by point throughout the essay. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source B: Paraphrased from A. J. P. Taylor, British historian, The Origins of the Second World War, 1961

Hitler was no more wicked and unscrupulous than many other contemporary statesmen. In principle and doctrine, he was no more wicked than other German leaders. He was a traditional German statesman, exploiting the opportunities offered to him by others.

Identify the main points that Source B makes about the causes of the Second World War in Europe, using details from the source.
items.answer: Hitler was an opportunist pursuing traditional German aims, exploiting chances given by other powers, rather than a uniquely wicked planner of war.
items.markingKey: Hitler was an opportunist pursuing traditional German aims, exploiting chances given by other powers, rather than a uniquely wicked planner of war. Award 1 mark for each relevant point drawn from the source, up to [2]. Points must come from the source itself; own knowledge is not credited in this question.

items.stem:

Hitler was no more wicked and unscrupulous than many other contemporary statesmen. In principle and doctrine, he was no more wicked than other German leaders. He was a traditional German statesman, exploiting the opportunities offered to him by others.

With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for an historian studying the causes of the Second World War in Europe.
items.answer: Value: A highly influential, provocative interpretation based on diplomatic documents. Limitations: Taylor relied mainly on published diplomatic papers and gave little weight to Hitler’s ideology; his provocative style may exaggerate.
items.markingKey: Value: A highly influential, provocative interpretation based on diplomatic documents. Limitations: Taylor relied mainly on published diplomatic papers and gave little weight to Hitler’s ideology; his provocative style may exaggerate. items.stem: A student claims that an “evaluate” essay only needs to list the strengths of a factor. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Evaluation requires weighing strengths and limitations and reaching a judgement.
items.markingKey: Evaluation requires weighing strengths and limitations and reaching a judgement. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Discuss the view that the Second World War in Europe was “Hitler’s war”.
items.answer: The war was primarily Hitler’s, though others’ decisions made it possible.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: intentionalist view of foreign policy; Taylor’s opportunism thesis; role of Britain, France and the USSR; structural causes from 1919. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: The war was primarily Hitler’s, though others’ decisions made it possible. Markbands – 13–15: clearly focused, well structured response; accurate and relevant knowledge used effectively; well-chosen examples; evaluation of different perspectives; all main points substantiated; reasoned, consistent conclusion; 10–12: clear awareness of the demands; clearly structured; accurate, relevant knowledge placed in context; analysis with most points substantiated; some awareness of different perspectives; 7–9: demands understood but not all implications considered; mostly accurate knowledge; some critical analysis, though partly narrative; 4–6: some indication of the demands; some knowledge but lacking accuracy or relevance; mostly narrative or descriptive, limited analysis; 1–3: little understanding of the demands of the question; poorly structured, little relevant knowledge, no analysis; 0: does not reach the standard of the descriptors below.

items.stem:
Source C: Paraphrased from Hugh Trevor-Roper, British historian, “A. J. P. Taylor, Hitler and the War”, Encounter, July 1961

Hitler’s war aims were consistent: the conquest of living space in the East, as set out in Mein Kampf and repeated in the Hossbach Memorandum of 1937. To call him an opportunist ignores his programme.

Evaluate Source C as evidence about the causes of the Second World War in Europe, considering its author, date, intended audience and content.
items.answer: Value: A direct rejoinder by a leading historian of Nazi Germany using ideological evidence. Limitations: It is a polemical review aimed at refuting Taylor, so it may underplay the role of opportunism and of other powers.

items.stem: Explain why it is important to identify the command term before planning an essay.
items.answer: The command term defines the task: “evaluate” requires weighing strengths and limitations, “compare and contrast” requires both cases throughout; misreading it leads to answers that do not meet the demands of the question.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "thesis"?
options: Make an appraisal by weighing up the strengths and limitations of an argument or factor
The central argument of an essay, stated clearly in the introduction and developed throughout
Give an account of the similarities and differences between two or more items or situations, referring to both throughout
Consider the merits or otherwise of an argument or concept, presenting a clear conclusion supported by evidence and sound argument
items.answer: The central argument of an essay, stated clearly in the introduction and developed throughout
items.markingKey: B. "thesis" is the central argument of an essay, stated clearly in the introduction and developed throughout.

items.stem: A student claims that the more facts an essay includes, the higher its mark. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Knowledge must be relevant and used to support analysis; unfocused detail does not raise the band.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the conclusion should not introduce new evidence.
items.answer: The conclusion should bring together the argument and give a reasoned judgement; new evidence belongs in the body where it can be analysed. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem: Using a plan for the question “To what extent was the weakness of the liberal state responsible for Mussolini’s rise to power?” as an example, explain the structure of a thesis-led essay with counter-argument.
items.answer: Thesis: weakness was the key condition but Fascist violence and elite support were decisive; paragraphs on liberal weakness, socio-economic crisis, Fascist methods and the king. The plan sets out a clear line of argument and places counter-arguments within a structure leading to a judgement.
items.markingKey: Context (Thesis: weakness was the key condition but Fascist violence and elite support were decisive; paragraphs on liberal weakness, socio-economic crisis, Fascist methods and the king.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: "A balanced essay must give exactly equal space to each side and avoid taking a position." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Balance means considering different views fairly; the essay must still reach a clear, supported judgement.
items.markingKey: Balance means considering different views fairly; the essay must still reach a clear, supported judgement. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

Source A: Paraphrased from Emilio Gentile, Italian historian, The Origins of Fascist Ideology 1918–1925, 1975

Fascism attracted genuine support among the middle classes, war veterans and students who saw it as a movement of national renewal against socialism and the discredited liberal politicians.

What does Source A suggest about the reasons for Mussolini’s rise to power? Refer closely to the source in your answer.
items.answer: Fascism had real popular support from groups seeking national renewal and opposing socialism.

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from Emilio Gentile, Italian historian, The Origins of Fascist Ideology 1918–1925, 1975

Fascism attracted genuine support among the middle classes, war veterans and students who saw it as a movement of national renewal against socialism and the discredited liberal politicians.

Source B: Paraphrased from Adrian Lyttelton, British historian, The Seizure of Power: Fascism in Italy 1919–1929, 1973

Fascism did not conquer power; it was handed to it. The king refused to sign the decree of martial law, and the army, which could have dispersed the marchers in hours, was never ordered to act.

“The weakness of the liberal state was the main reason for Mussolini’s rise to power.” Using Sources A and B and your own knowledge, how far do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Liberal weakness was the essential precondition, but Fascist violence and elite support turned it into Mussolini’s appointment.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – supporting: trasformismo and unstable coalitions; failure to deal with the biennio rosso; king’s refusal to declare martial law. Challenging: squadristi violence; Fascist appeal to the middle class and veterans; support from industrialists and landowners; Mussolini’s leadership. Judgement: Liberal weakness was the essential precondition, but Fascist violence and elite support turned it into Mussolini’s appointment. items.stem:
Source A: Photograph of Fidel Castro’s arrival in Havana, 8 January 1959, published internationally (description)

[Photograph] Fidel Castro, rifle on his shoulder, addresses a huge crowd in Havana, January 1959; banners read “Viva Fidel” and “Libertad”.

Source B: Photograph of the “Day of Potsdam”, 21 March 1933, widely reproduced in Nazi propaganda (description)

[Photograph] Hitler, in a suit, bows and shakes hands with President Hindenburg, in military uniform, at the Garrison Church in Potsdam, 21 March 1933.

In what ways do Sources A and B agree and disagree about the rise of authoritarian leaders in different regions?
items.answer: Both images show new leaders seeking legitimacy in 1933 and 1959. Castro’s legitimacy comes from mass popular support and his armed victory, whereas Hitler’s comes from the endorsement of the traditional elite; one is revolutionary, the other presented as traditional and legal.
items.markingKey: Both images show new leaders seeking legitimacy in 1933 and 1959. Source A: Paraphrased from A. J. P. Taylor, British historian, The Origins of the Second World War, 1961

Source B: Paraphrased from Hugh Trevor-Roper, British historian, “A. J. P. Taylor, Hitler and the War”, Encounter, July 1961

Hitler’s war aims were consistent: the conquest of living space in the East, as set out in Mein Kampf and repeated in the Hossbach Memorandum of 1937. To call him an opportunist ignores his programme.

In what ways do Sources A and B agree and disagree about the causes of the Second World War in Europe?
items.answer: Both focus on Hitler’s role in causing the war. Taylor sees him as a traditional opportunist exploiting others’ mistakes, while Trevor-Roper sees him as pursuing a consistent programme of conquest; one minimises Hitler’s unique responsibility, the other stresses it.

[Photograph] Fidel Castro, rifle on his shoulder, addresses a huge crowd in Havana, January 1959; banners read “Viva Fidel” and “Libertad”.

Source B: Photograph of the “Day of Potsdam”, 21 March 1933, widely reproduced in Nazi propaganda (description)
